review: Games don't scare me. Movies don't scare me. In fact, short of being dropped in the middle of the ocean or singing in public, there's not much I'm bothered by... except Amnesia. Why? Because in this game, I am powerless. I cannot fight back. Games like Doom, Resident Evil, Dead Space, etc.; They fail to send chills up my spine and make me squeal like a child because they made the mistake of giving me an arsenal of weapons and badass personality traits. Are Isaac Clarke and Claire Redfield afraid? Sure, and I don't blame them. But I'm not, because I look awesome and I can materialize various tools of immenent destruction. Those creepers waiting to pop-out from behind the corner aren't trying to scare me, they're sacrificing themselves to the God of Death! Amnesia, though... My tools are the world's worst lantern and a number of closets to hide in! I couldn't fight if my life depended on it, and it most certainly does. Well done, Amnesia; I haven't looked over my shoulder this much since I was 12.

[b]Amnesia: still the ruling king of horror games[/b]

Horror games are a special genre. What scares one person to hell, could make somebody else just raise an eyebrow, or even come across as comical to yet another gamer. Opinions on what makes a good horror game do vary accordingly, but amidst all these discussions, there's one game that stands out: [i]Amnesia: The Dark Descent[/i]. Almost everybody who has played this game, concedes that it is exceptionally scary, and thus succeeds wonderfully as a horror game.

The first of the two [i]Amnesia[/i] games, it was released just five years ago, in september 2010. It's not the first horror game by its developer, Frictional Games, who earlier made the [i]Penumbra[/i] games, but it's certainly the title that made Frictional Games famous. With the hype around the upcoming release of [i]Soma[/i], yet another Frictional title, playing through their best known horror game yet only seemed appropriate, and long overdue.

Actually I started this game already three times earlier this year, every time not finding the courage to move on after the first hour or so, out of pure fear. I only play this kind of games when it's dark outside, using headphones, in order to let them develop their full scaring potential, but with [i]Amnesia: The Dark Descent[/i] this kind of approach just looked impossible. The past couple of weeks I finally found the courage to persevere (in complete darkness), but I was only able to play the game in small pieces, only half an hour or so on end, after which I literally had to recover.

This may seem like exaggerated, but it's not. This game is by far the scariest I've ever played. Playing as Daniel, you have to re-discover who you are and what you're doing in a medieval castle somewhere deep in the German woods. As the game progresses, the story poses more and more questions, and only at the very end did all the pieces come together for me. But it's not the story itself that's particularly scary. It's the way the game puts the player in an extremely vulnerable position, without any means of defense (no swords or guns in this one!) and only some tinderboxes and a lantern as a means to progress through the increasingly unsettling surroundings.

The game is by far the darkest I've ever played. Darkness is actually transformed into one of the game's defining elements: when standing in darkness, Daniel slowly but surely turns mad, and the only way to counter this is either to light some candles with the tinderboxes, or to light your lantern. Since lantern oil is quite scarce, I found myself constantly trying to save it as much as possible. There is a constant looming danger in the form of monsters, who are seldomly to been seen but impose terror upon the player by sound or just by thought. For when a monster finds you, it's almost surely instant death. The game manages to strike the perfect balance between slowly progressing episodes where I was fumbling around in the dark, hiding for monsters and looking for clues or letters, and some scenes where the only option was: run!

It's hard to describe in words exactly why this game got so deep under my skin, though, because it terrified me on an even deeper level that has nothing to do with graphics or game mechanics. I think the theme of man turning into a monster even worse than any monster imagineable struck a resonating chord inside me. I found myself screaming out loud at times, mostly out of utter disgust at what was happening. The game had a very unsettling effect on my, and probably that's why it took me several tries to play and finish it. It's a masterpiece in its genre, yet to be trumped.

[b]Very highly recommended, but not for the faint of heart, nor for heart patients[/b]

Similar to the Penumbra games, Amnesia: TDD is all about atmosphere and storytelling.  The biggest difference between the two series is that Amnesia does include more of the classic horror induced moments of being chased and hunted.  Not that Penumbra didn't have a bit of that, but I'd say in Amnesia, there were specific moments designed to inject some action.

Overall however, the game is paced similarly.  I could wander about, sip some coffee, read my notes and mementos and take in my surroundings.  
This may sound casual but what Amnesia succeeds in doing is creating a sense of dread.  Brennenburg Castle is a miserable place and rarely do you find yourself feeling too comfortable. When an enemy does discover you and then gives chase, it is probably one of the more scary moments I've experienced in a game.  The music, the blurriness of your view, the sound of the monster chasing you...not to mention, when you do finally get behind a closed door and find a hiding spot, you then get to watch as the door is violently brought down into pieces. All you can do is hope you're not spotted as you stare at the wall (there is a "sanity" element if you're new to these games).  IRL, I am guilty of some audible "gasping" during these moments.  During one particular chase I couldn't find an adequate path to get away from my pursuer and let out a frightened yelp that I am ashamed to even admit. Though, it is important to mention that I allowed the game to get under my skin purely because it was better that way.  I could have played it and completely steeled myself from letting it get to me (e.g. left the lights on, lowered the sound, casually approached the objectives), but what's fun about that?  For me, nothing.

As far as the story is concerned, I felt compelled to move forward to find the next clue.  I could feel a bit of excitement (or perhaps it's better described as relief) every time I saw a new note to read or completed a puzzle.  Naturally I won't reveal any spoilers just in case someone does read this review. 

I must emphasize that this is not a game full of jump scares and over the top gore.  With that being said, there are some very disturbing scenes that you come across.  I walk away from this game still thinking about some of what I experienced. Not just from the imagery but the story in general. Per the recommendation from the developers when you first start the game, play with the lights off, don't worry about saving and allow the story to drive you forward.

This game is 11 years old and a lot of people know about it thanks to the classic horror let's plays by famous youtubers, but here are my thoughts anyway :

Story > You are a man who wakes up in a strange dark castle and has no idea what's going on or how he got there. So you have to figure it out by exploring and finding several notes and clues throughout the game. I personally love the plot of the game. It slowly reveals itself and has a good pace. There is also much additional lore in the world of Amnesia.

Gameplay > You can only run and hide which rises the tension and horror very well. Most parts of the game are very dark and staying in the dark slowly drives you mad. Your only friends are tinderboxes and a lantern. You can move, rotate and throw almost any object. The puzzles are quite simple but very very satisfying to solve. The scariness not only comes from the bizarre events and creatures, but also from the gloomy, dark, haunting atmosphere itself.

Soundtrack & Audio > The sounds you hear from enemies and other sources are quite scary and can also help you avoid danger and solve puzzles. The soundtrack fits the game perfectly and is memorable. I really like the chase music and the ones you hear when an enemy is nearby. The voice acting is perfect.

Length and Replayability > It took me around 7-8 hours to complete the main story even though I'm a bit dumb when it comes to puzzle solving, so you could assume that it's a bit short but you wouldn't feel that way. There are multiple endings that you can get without having to start over. There's also a challenging game mode and a small DLC with an interesting plot. But my personal favorite has to be the custom stories. You can get hundreds of hours of playtime by playing different stories made by the players and there's always something new to try.

Other > Although I have a potato computer, the game ran smoothly and I didn't encounter any bugs except one time that a box just glitched out of existence but it wasn't game breaking. Graphics look good even after a decade of release. The price is totally ok but I always recommend waiting for a sale even for a 2$ game.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is an excellent and memorable horror game that is totally worth your time. 100% Recommended.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent, a game that caused quite a stir when it was released, thanks to its fresh take on horror and its (numerous) YouTube videos.

But what makes Amnesia a good game?

First of all, its atmosphere – eerie, cold, dark and medieval – transports you to another world, another era. In fact, the castle reminds me a bit of Bram Stoker’s Dracula’s castle.

As well as its gripping atmosphere, the gameplay is also very immersive: moving the mouse to open drawers and doors, hiding in cupboards… All of this plunges us straight into the heart of the action (or rather, the horror).

Then, of course, there’s the story, which you uncover as you play alongside the character (remember, our character suffers from amnesia at the start); it’s superbly written and captivating, well worth reading – and even re-reading at the end to fully understand everything.

All these elements make Amnesia a sublime and gripping horror game which, despite its fairly short base playtime, can still provide hours of thrills thanks to the option to add ‘Custom Stories’ found online.

[h1] I don't know what to say exactly, as I have no memory... I only found a letter stating this... [/h1]

Today, at almost 30 years old, I finished Amnesia: The Dark Descent for the first time. It all started in 2011, when we gathered our friends to play together, and I heard about this game for the first time. We loved to unite the guys together to play, especially horror games and we had heard that nothing beat this one. We were just teenagers, and we'd played some very scary games, but this one was so surprisingly strong, no one could even bear to watch directly, I was the only one who dares to play alone. With the little courage we had at the time, we only went to the Wine Cellar part, from there we alternated between the menu, desperately quitting the game, opening it again and the cycle repeating itself.

I decided to pick up the game again 12 years later. The reasons were curiosity (if the game is still as terrifying as it was at the time), fascination with the story (even though I know little), and also because of this remarkable experience of mine as a teenager. After finishing the game, 12 years later, I share here the following updated findings with great sincerity and impartiality. First, we start with the [b] GRAPHICS [/b]. The game is a little dated, and for that I implemented a remaster made by a fan, which is widely used and known by the community, which gave the game an excellent upgrade compared to the original. Without a doubt, it doesn't compare to today's graphics and mechanics, but nothing that hinders your experience. The game is perfectly playable nowadays, not to mention that the lack of light in the game helps and alleviates a lot in terms of level of details, especially those with greater distance.

Now the second factor, [b] ATMOSPHERE [/b]. I don't think any other horror game I've played until this day compares to Amnesia: The Dark Descent. Perhaps Resident Evil (the 1st Remake) and Silent Hill 2 are the closest, but it really involves another complexity. The game is too dark. It has extremely uncomfortable ambient sounds, such as screams of torture, children's cries, creaking wood, footsteps and agonizing moans. Something truly diabolical. Resources, especially oil, are scarce in the game, and must be used in moderation, which induces the player to perform actions with a certain anxiety and accelerated pace, making you “throw yourself” into the unknown and macabre environments of the scenario without know what awaits you. Finally, something that doesn't get talked about much and deserves real applause and recognition. The soundtrack... the game's soundtrack/sound effects are simply FANTASTIC. They fit perfectly with each segment of the game. Moments of hope, terrifying moments, characters, environment, chase, complete mastery.

Third factor, atmosphere. I don't think any oth... oops... I just remembered, that was already written... now is the part where we will deal with the [b] ENEMIES [/b] of the game. The monsters.... ahhhh the monsters... how to define them? They are horrible, grotesque, with bizarre movements and soul-shuddering sounds. Add this to the darkness and the environment around you and the impact is powerful. To this day, I believe that no other creature has ever given me such chills. Furthermore, they do not appear so frequently, a factor that means that the quality of construction of moments is prioritized, causing greater apprehension and anxiety. This entire set makes each encounter desperate, unpredictable and remarkable. As you progress through the game, you will better understand how the mechanics and stealth through monsters work, reducing the tension level a little and increasing your confidence and courage.

Fourth and penultimate factor, [b] ENVIRONMENT/SETTING [/b]. Here, in my opinion, is where the game's creators rocks. The game takes place in 1839, in Brennenburg Castle, Prussia. This era has a lot of historical inspiration from the Middle Ages and the Enlightenment. The level of creativity and intelligence to set a horror game in an ancient era with historical involvement is brilliant! An extremely rich idea, opening up a river of possibilities and elements that were masterfully introduced into the game. A dark and gigantic castle, lamps, candles, books, potions, tonics, paintings, chains, barrels, everything perfectly placed. Imagine a time when science was moving in short steps... everything was uncertain, mysterious. Science or Witchcraft? Alchemy or Magic? All concepts were hypothetical, undefined. All this air of mysticism can be defined as a touch of elegance introduced to the game. All historical elements and settings are the foundation, the soul of the game that encapsulates all the previously mentioned terror and atmosphere.

Finally, [b] STORY/CHARACTERS [/b]. I can't believe I've come this far..., but I must continue with courage and determination to finish my review. The game takes place only in the castle, but the story begins long ago before the game. Thanks to the amnesia, the game captivates us to look for all the pieces of the puzzle with determination and enthusiasm. Why we woke up like this, why we have to kill the castle baron, why horrible things happened, and so on. As you progress through the game, things start to become clearer and all your questions are gradually answered. The fact that we continue even when we shouldn't, directly concerns the mold and personality of the character Daniel, who you controls.

Daniel is a fantastic character, who needs to go on a true hero's journey. Loaded with guilt and remorse, but with convictions and steely courage to determinedly achieve redemption and the incessant search for good at all costs. Antagonist or Protagonist? Villain or Hero? I don't remember anymore... it's up to you... just like... Alexander, the game's other notable character. Alexander is the stereotypical powerful and wise man. As Daniel himself mentions: ‘’A Renaissance man, like Da Vinci’’. Alexander is the man who sets out to help Daniel with his curse, offering his knowledge and technological advances in exchange for his service. But why then should we kill him? Should we kill the only man who offered us help? You will have to unravel these questions on your own... So I wish you good luck on your journey to discover the truth.

[h1] FINAL VERDICT[/h1] What to say about Amnesia The Dark Descent then? A good, short and simple horror game? No! A LEGENDARY horror game! responsible for catapulting the careers of many famous YouTubers in the past, and who should pay their respects. A game with a thrilling story, captivating characters, iconic enemies, remarkable moments of terror and emotion, and everything can be proven by the testimony above. For me, it's the most iconic horror game in gaming history. If not, it is undoubtedly on the same shelf as Resident Evil and Silent Hill 2. My passion aside, it has been and continues to be chosen, by the general public and critics, as one of the best horror games in the gaming history and also the scariest game ever made. A good horror game gives you scares and fear, but a legendary horror game gives you an unforgettable, exciting and perpetual experience!

[b] (Don’t) Play with all the lights off. [/b]
[b] (Don’t) Play alone. [/b]

I actually do reviews for games on Giant Bomb and PC Gamer... and one game I have trouble reviewing is Amnesia Dark Decent. It's not that I'm indecisive it's just, I can't find the proper words to ever describe this game. You couldn't possibly understand what this game means to me. You might like it and the horror genre would say it's a great game but to me it's more. This game single handedly restored my faith in horror games and got me playing them again. After Resident Evil 5/6 and after Silent Hill Homecoming and Downpour I stopped. Stopped playing, stopped reading up on, stopped caring about horror games. Resident Evil I saw coming but Silent Hill too? This mass appeal mindless action bullsh*t needs to stop. Survival horror was the genre that got me into gaming and then I saw the genre just up and leave us fans for more sales from the Call of Duty players. Action is where it's at? As the head developer for Resi 6 said "Survival Horror games are no longer popular, we needed a new direction and new ideas" well guess what... Amnesia proved Survival Horror still has plenty of new ideas to bring to the genre and proved that the genre is not dead. 
 
Amnesia is art.... it's artwork crafted by brilliant minds. Look past all the fun scary chases and the jumpscares, just look at the game. A first person game that doesn't have weapons? Yeah imagine that. You hide and run from monsters, much like people would do in real life. But if you break down the level design, the choice of imagery, the methodically detailed environments. You will see true beauty within. If I may quote some negative reviews here "water monster wasn't all that great of an enemy, he doesn't even have a character design. It's lazy...." yes they had limited resources however this isn't lazy design choices. The fact that you cannot see the water monster is more terrifying than any other creature in the game. It plays off your imagination, the fear of the unknown. Your mind subconsciously filled the blank with your worst fear which gave this monster so much memorability. The water monster is one of the most memorable moments, everyone talks about it and that's the reason. 
 
After such a horrifying experience with the water monster, what happens? You walk into a well light room with a fountain that supplies the calming sound of running water, a hole in the ceiling with light seeping through (one of the first times you see the light of day in this game), beautiful music plays softly in the background and the room has a tint of blue in the air. This is no randomly designed room, no this is a reward. This is saying "Hey you made it through that horrible experience, breathe relax a bit. You deserve it" and that is something I haven't seen before. No stupid achievement unlocked, no legendary loot, no high score and no misspelled CONGRADURATIONS. In a game that plays on your fear and emotions, they reward with such. They made you crap your pants, now they're making you feel relaxed. And that means more than any achievement. 
 
The story is rich and it plays along with the tension in the game. The enemies aren't scary on the level of a jumpscare but rather the fear of being chased. Jumpscares are cheap thrills, true fear is much harder to achieve in a gamer and much more satisfying for the gamer. They accomplish this in many ways. Never knowing what danger lurks beyond the glow of your lamp, the dark abyss continuously hunts you down, the monsters are not just some scary looking monsters for the sake of "boo look at me I'm scary" they're people you tortured and sacrificed for your own safety against the darkness, their disfigured bodies are representations of the guilt you bare in the deepest parts of your conscious despite suffering Amnesia you still feel it, led astray by someone you thought you could trust, no escape or easy way out the only path is down and it's bathed in darkness as you descend slowly into your past with each step you lost sanity, walls are shaking, the crackling sound of your own mind is louder than your beating heart as you're chased by a horrifying disfigured creature you created, the sound of screeching can be heard when they're getting closer letting you know how close you are to death. 
 
Oh... jeez I... I can go on and on about this game. Hell I want too... but if this gets any longer it will be considered a novel. The best thing I can say about this game? Play it... please. I beg you if you're a fan of horror games, if you like being scared, if you like a good story or immersion or hell if you just want to play a damn good game; play this game! 
 
This is without a doubt my favorite game of all time. The favorite game, not one of. That's hard to say, but it's true. I never game 10 out of 10. I always made fun of other reviewers who did, saying no game is perfect. 10 out of 10 is saying it's the masterpiece of all gaming and cannot be improved in any way, shape or form. However, I've seen my mistake. You don't give it a 10 based on some score that means nothing to anyone else other than you. You're giving it a 10 based on the experience the game gave you. And based on that, Amnesia The Dark Decent was given my very first 10 out of 10.

I have been debating on making a review for this game and I've finally decided to. This is going to be a long one, because I have a lot to say about this game. I'll be splitting this review up into parts, and talking about each individually. 

Game-play: 

Amnesia's base game offers a very strong horror experience, which in my opinion still holds up today. The game does a very good job of getting you immersed in its dark grisly world, and then proceeding to scare the crap out of you until you feel as broken as Daniel. Honestly it's hard to complete in one sitting, it personally took me 3 weeks to finish it my first time back in 2014. The story is a bit hard to grasp if you are rushing through the game, but if you take your time to look for and read notes, you'll find it much easier to understand. 

The environments in Amnesia is one of the main reasons why it is so scary. The dark, sometimes disturbing locations, the ambiance, the anticipation for anything to jump out at you, it's perfect.  

Having to manage sanity and oil can be a little bit tedious at times, but if you are careful to light up areas, and conserve oil you'll probably be fine.  

The puzzles in amnesia are sometimes a little weak, but it doesn't really have to much of an impact on the overall game-play I feel. 


Custom stories (the best part): 

This is in my opinion the main reason to get this game, and the reason for my egregiously long playtime. Custom stories are community made mods for amnesia, allowing people to basically make their own horror games using the medium of amnesia. It's a joy to see what people come up with, and experience the stories they wish to tell. There are countless custom stories out there, and I'll provide a list of my recommendations at the end of this review. 


Game files: 

This is a little bonus thing I find fun to mess around with sometimes. All of amnesia's files are able to be edited, such as configuration files, audio files, images etc. meaning you can customize almost everything about the game. You can replace music with songs from another game, make monsters speak, make it so your lantern doesn't consume oil and emits blue light, you can even give Daniel a different voice, the possibilities are endless. 

I strongly recommend making backups of any files you are going to edit 

If you are going to replace audio files, I recommend using audacity to convert your sounds to .ogg 

if you are going to replace images, I personally just use an online converter so you don't have to pay to convert to .tga 

Config files are easy to edit, you just need any text editor. 

Also, your changes will carry over to any custom stories you have as well 


My custom story recommendation list: 

Some of my favorite custom stories, you can find them all on moddb 

Must plays: 

The ones you’ve just gotta play 

Amadeus – Your brother is stolen, and you must find him. 

Wow, just wow. The quality this custom story offers is unrivaled. Definitely a must play. 

Simulacrum – A monk journey’s to “The Spout.” 

One of my personal favorites. The story is a bit difficult to understand but the game-play is great, with unique puzzles and environments. love it. 

Destiny Rebellion/Destiny Revenant – A man attempts to change his destiny. 

Play these two if you are looking for a unique experience you won't get from any other custom story. 

The Great Work – You stumble across an orb fragment, and get roped into things much bigger than you. 

Great, easy to understand story with unique puzzles and good game-play. 

Five magics – You seek to stop someone from abusing the orb’s power. 

If you enjoyed The Great Work, you'll enjoy this too. 

Final Revelations (Remastered) - You attempt to uncover the mystery of the Crusader’s. 

If you are looking for a good custom story with a long playtime, this is for you. It introduces many new features such as NPCs, shops, a morality system, day/night, and much more.  

Key to Freedom – You are offered freedom in exchange for a key, deep within a manor. 

Just an overall great custom story. 

Amnesia: Rain – You awake trapped within a castle, and must escape. 

Loved the story, and the twist at the end. 

The Subconscious Trials – You are offered 500,000 dollars to participate in a medical trial. 

Good story, good game-play. Nice. 

Those Who Were Forgotten – You are tossed into the sewers as punishment for crimes you didn’t commit 

Heavily underrated in my opinion. Good puzzles and atmosphere, good voice acting, good story, the only issue really is the very difficult to get good ending, but you can find a guide for it in the custom stories files if you are having trouble. 

A Late Night Drink – You grab a drink, late at night. 

The one everybody knows. Very good.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is one of those games that only comes around once all of the planets in our solar system align perfectly - which, is to say, never. But yet Amnesia did come around, and it redefined not just the horror genre itself, but indie gaming as a whole, I think. It showed that first-person gaming fit the horror experience perfectly (in my opinion, even demonstrating that first-person horror is the best possible kind of horror), and with the right narrative and thematic techniques (in both writing and gameplay), could create a rich and beautifully dark universe for the player to inhabit. 

... Assuming the player actually is bad enough to launch the game in the first place, that is. There's no two ways about it: Amnesia is one of the most terrifying games ever created, and that's as much a byproduct of its powerful and compellingly grim story as much as it is a byproduct of its grueling and sinister gameplay. At points you will be overwhelmingly afraid to continue playing, simply because every action and every moment you spend interacting with it, you realize more and more how powerless and incapable you are, and how little resources you really have. There is no combat in Amnesia - there is only survival, and it's as fleeting as it is difficult.

It's not the game for everyone, but I think that all gamers should at least try to experience it; even the first half of it, if not more. It may take you months to accomplish, but a full playthrough of Amnesia can be one of the most rewarding and exhilarating experiences in the history of gaming.

Surrounded by the dark castle walls of Brennenburg, ridden with amnesia and haunted by an ominous shadow, you lie awake questioning your sanity and the daunting task ahead of you.

At release, Amnesia: The Dark Descent quickly became an iconic pillar of the "Let's Play" genre on YouTube, arguably making the platform's most notable stars such as PewDiePie and the like, famous. Aside from that, it had a massive impact on the horror genre that gave birth to a whole new generation of games in order to emulate its initial success. The formula was simple; strip all power from the player and force them to hide from the monsters. While most games bombard you with seeing the monster up close and personal, here you are penalized and thus the novelty is maintained. Although the foundation is simple, there is complexity in the mechanics that is best left for the player to discover.

A true horror in the making without expectation of big climactic cutscenes and endings; Amnesia instead, relies on sound, providing a permanent unsettling rumble as if the castle itself was moaning and groaning. The game reeks of atmosphere and capitalizes on continuous tension rather than jump scares. This is a must play.

[h1]The Dark Descent[/h1]

[b]I recently replayed Amnesia: The Dark Descent as it got updated with achievements and decided to write a review afterwards. Amnesia: TDD is an amazing horror game packed with interesting and challenging puzzles, a very eerie atmosphere and dangerous monsters.[/b]


Ingame you have a health and a sanity level, hiding in the darkness decreases your sanity but makes it harder for monsters to spot you, staying near light or lighting your lantern stops your sanity from decreasing but allows monsters to easily spot you, solving puzzles and progressing increases your sanity if you have lost any, but looking at monsters decreases it as well. Once you have gone completely insane you break down on the floor and can't move for a few seconds, this makes it incredibly easy for monsters to get you if there are any around, after getting up again your sanity will be restored to the best possible level. Being hit by a monster or environmental hazard decreases your health which can be refilled with Laudanum, a chemical you can rarely find ingame. Besides Laudanum there are multiple other things you can find, those things include tinderboxes, which can be used to light light sources, notes, which can be read, oil, which can be used to refill your lantern, and various other, mostly puzzle related items. The monsters wander around the levels searching for you, they are attracted by light and sounds, so you should be quiet and avoid lights around them. You'll know when they're around though thanks of the grotesque noises they make. If they spot you they start chasing you, so you better hide quickly because they're faster than you as well! There's also another type of monster that behaves completely different than the others, which you'll have to find for yourself if you do decide to play the game! 

The gameplay mechanics above result in the game being hard but balanced, you can hide in the dark but if you stay there for too long you'll have to suffer the consequences, using your lantern gives you a mobile but limited light source which can be turned off if necessary, but staying near a light source lit by a tinderbox or a natural light source will not consume your precious oil but could put you in a more dangerous situation. While there are a lot of parts where these horrifying creatures hunt you, sadly there are also a lot of boring parts where not all that much is happening, it would've probably been better if the different creatures appeared more often, especially during puzzles, although that could just be me.

Another thing that this game is quite popular for is its amazing physics engine which allows you to interact with almost any object by either taking and throwing it around (small objects), by pushing/pulling it (larger objects) or by opening/closing it (doors and drawers). This results in many precious items being hidden behind a few barrels or inside a drawer and is required in many puzzles. Additionally throwing a box at a monster can give you precious seconds in an intense chase as it stuns the monster for a short period of time.

The story is very deep and interesting and I never skipped a note thinking it would not be worth my time reading the note. The notes generally explain the story very well and pretty much everything is explained throughout the game. I won't go into much detail describing the story itself as that would ruin the fun in exploring it yourself, the store page already provides the necessary story elements. There are three different endings.

Atmosphere is probably one of the strongest elements of this game, not only will the soundscape give you goosebumps but the tension you feel when being chased by a monster or the fear you feel when a monster is walking by is unmet by any other game I've played.

The puzzles are always challenging and interesting and solving them feels satisfying. Especially good are the puzzles you have to solve while monsters are around, these puzzles, besides the atmosphere, are one of the greatest elements in Amnesia. While the puzzles are definitely not easy they are never unsolvable and never break the immersion, you'll always have an idea of what you have to do and if not then a little looking around will give you the hint you need.

While the graphics are definitely dated they are still quite acceptable and especially the light effects look very nice. The monsters look disgusting and really give you the creeps.

The price of 19.99€ totally justifies the average completion time of 10 hours, especially considering the general quality of the game in addition to the free "Justine" DLC and the "Remember" story collection (both of which I will take a look at later) packed with the game. Besides that, due to the freely available in-house HPL 2 engine which the game uses, players are able to create and distribute custom storys which others can download and play, these are officially supported and can be loaded ingame, this allows for infinite horror!


[b]In conclusion, Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a masterpiece in game design and a must-have for every horror fan, with amazing puzzles and gameplay, a deep story, an incredible atmosphere, nightmare-inducing monsters and the ability to create custom stories which makes the fun endless![/b]

[h1]Summary[/h1]

+Great Atmosphere (Great music, Graphics, and theme)
+Great Pacing
+Great Mechanics 
+Good Puzzles 

[h1]Fear Itself[/h1]

It is so well focused on all the elements on horror that you are unable to even fight back at the enemy. Forever doomed to listen and feel terror down your spine as you try to find cover or some place to take shelter from the sight of the enemy. 

Another feature of this game to note is the idea of looking at your enemy makes you panic is quite genius. This allows for more realistic scare tactics such as quick glimpses of the enemy, and constantly trying to avoid its attention. 

[h1]Issues[/h1]

While Amnesia is a good horror game there are some glaring faults with the overall game that could makes  the game lose the effectiveness of its horror. Continue reading at your own risk.

[h1]Predictability[/h1]

The issue stems from the predictability of the monsters spawning right after puzzles. Once you realize you're safe doing a puzzle you lose the tension and prepare even beforehand for the enemy to spawns by memorizing some closet locations. When a player sees the pattern the threat itself ceases to be horrifying. 

[h1]Confrontation[/h1]

The other issue is simply when players choose to confront enemies. Seeing the enemy also takes away to the mystery of what they look like and actually brings down the scare factor. Once they figure out how to trick the AI in more ways or simply stop being so afraid. The game design choices have been good to avoid this happening except for the fact that randomized monsters poof once you confront/die to them and you are pretty much safe till next puzzle.

[h1]Flashbacks[/h1]

Flashbacks do not restructure the place to how it would look like before the guy had amnesia. It would be a better visual comparison to see how much the place suffered structurally as a result. 

[h1]Taking Control away[/h1]

Taking control away from the player to demonstrate how the character feels at the moment I feel was a mistake. They do this a few times in the game instead of letting the player himself/herself react. For example in the start of the game when you hear noises above you, your character will fall to the ground with his face near it. I found this really overdramatic and not needed for the already well established atmosphere in this game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Overall Amensia despite all the flaws that can occur, is a great horror game that tries its best to put fear in you and prolong the scare with smart tactics that are not blatent jump scares.

Back in 2011, while spending some time in Copenhagen, a conversation at a party led to an unexpected introduction to Frictional Games from Sweden. A guy there very eager to talk, brought up the game Penumbra: Overture, claiming to know the developers. Although he had spent a lot of time playing the game, he confessed that he never really liked it. He went on to elaborate on his reasons, but his in-depth critique was difficult to grasp, especially since the game was unfamiliar to me and he was already a bit tipsy.

Life on tour back then meant gaming mostly happened at friends’ places or on my PlayStation Portable, which I always carried with me. I remember playing games like LEGO Star Wars, LocoRoco and Patapon. Amnesia: The Dark Descent later caught my attention, particularly due to its font, which evoked heavy metal aesthetics. A game store clerk however, dismissed any connection to metal and labeled it dull, leading to a different, now-forgotten purchase instead.
Some time ago, I was specifically searching for low-spec games and since Amnesia has more or less become one of them now, I've finally had the chance to play it myself, so here’s what I think about it.

The oppressive atmosphere and intense tension are really well executed, largely thanks to the unsettling sound design. While some audio elements could have been more authentic, and there are moments where they don’t quite fit, the overall work here is undeniably strong. Enjoyed the subtle and psychological horror style as well, it’s not exactly for those who always crave action and combat, but I find it refreshing when a game takes a different approach. Being constantly on guard and hiding heightens the sense of vulnerability, making the game even more suspenseful.

The story unfolds gradually through notes and flashbacks. At times, it feels a bit disjointed, but it raises some moral questions and delves into disturbing themes. Unfortunately by the halfway point, I had grown so accustomed to everything that nothing really shocked me anymore. And then there was a moment in the game where a grotesque creature with a broken mouth was hanging around, engaging in a polite conversation with me while repeatedly saying the same things, it was pretty ridiculous.

In my humble opinion, anyone who enjoys horror games and hasn't played Amnesia yet should give it a try, the chances are high that you'll like it. I've marked the second game: A Machine for Pigs, and will catch up on it sometime in the future.

Will it prepare you for Amnesia: The Dark Descent? Probably not.
You play as Daniel, a man we initially know precious little about, and not in a good way either. We are in a castle that would probably be cozy, if not of the atmosphere and sound around us. We soon find out Daniel fears the dark and there's something... more to this. We explore the hallways and rooms, finding notes to help us make sense of this world. Soon enough we find a note to self. It tells us that:
We chose to forget how we ended up here.
We must kill Alexander of Brennenburg
A Shadow is chasing us, a living nightmare.
With that we begin our dark descent.

The gameplay unravels with ponderous but constant pace. You have your stats, inventory, health... and sanity. Pretty soon we are introduced to some of the strongest sides of the game: The light/dark interplay with sanity. You gain sanity by progressing in game. You lose it by witnessing disturbing events, staring at enemies and staying in the dark. You're told the lower the sanity, the harder it is to deal with enemies. That they'll be alerted if it drops to zero. Sanity alters your perception of reality as it drops: your vision gets blurry and distorted, portraits and other objects change form, hallucinations escalate, sometimes you even hallucinate enemies. On top of the excellently made atmosphere, it can make your play a living hell indeed.
 As you progress, if you are thorough, you find tinderboxes to light up torches and candles, and lamp oil for your mobile lantern. You will also find notes to further explain the setting. Much stress will result from the dilemma of preserving sanity or expending the lamp oil with your lantern and/or tinderboxes.

The game rewards those who dare to risk sanity-harming events. You'll find more useful items and be able to appreciate the story more. It is best played cautiously, fearfully, diligently. As you progress, the game will introduce enemies to you: First meekly and from far away, but don't let it deceive you: Half the horror in game comes from your inability to fight the enemies. You can only hide and wait till they leave. You have options: Will you lose sanity to hiding in the dark, turning your fear into your friend? Depending on situation, you'll be trying to hide in rooms, in the dark, be as far away as possible, or will have no choice but to run away in harrowing chase. An occasional puzzle will bring some variety. The game is divided into many levels. It starts linear, but then introduces hubs, from where batches of levels are available to be tackled in any order, barring prequisite items to unlock access. As you proceed towards your goal and explore, the veil of amnesia will slowly wear off. You'll slowly realize who Daniel is, what was he up to, and the motivations and artifacts of those around him. This game features some of the most depraved and inhuman characters around, and to your and Daniel's distress, their works will be expressed here. On your journey, the Shadow, manifested in fleshy residue, will continue to follow you, as if chasing you. Without spoiling too much, let me just say: It is not an enemy. It's something arguably worse.

The evils we witness, the atmosphere, the constant and heavy sense of dread, would not be possible without a stellar sound design. Mikko Tarmia has crafted the OST with loving care, and the sounds you hear all make the horror of it all possible. The events we witness (from mere gust of wind to The Shadow going ham somewhere), the hallucinations of Daniel (there's gonna be plenty of that), even psychic attacks: The game revels in trolling you and teasing you with threat of danger, making you scare yourself, especially when it'd only make things worse. Yet much like the darkness, sound design will be your asset. The enemies are loud, and sound will be your main way to locate them.

The presentation is clearly from early 2010s, with pitiful but servicable textures for these days, and lighting from that era as well. It has its charm and will not stand in the way of you being engaged.
You will witness damp rusty sewers, castle hallways, storage areas, all in the usual rustic castle style. But as you progress, you witness spaces that are either beautiful, claustrophobic and disturbing, or otherworldly in its presentation. Machinery fitting 19th century will often be seen, and be object of progression or puzzles.

This is the game where danger lurks when you don't know what you're doing, but this fear can be overcome. As you go, you will start to know what you're doing, and how to handle encounters. You will harden, but the depravity of what you witness will only escalate. In the end, you will truly have made your dark descent, into what defined Daniel's misery. Will you turn your thoughts to vengeance? Or something more?

A maddening, but ultimately sublime experience. Face a game that made history of the genre. Unveil guilt and hearken for redemption as your sins pile up. Help someone and maybe be helped. Settle a debt and conquer your fears. All this and more in Amnesia: The Dark Descent.

A very well crafted title by Frictional Games. Rating: 9/10

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a first-person survival-horror adventure game developed by Frictional Games for the HPL Engine 2. Following the perspective of Daniel, a 19th century explorer, the player begins the game without any memories and is forced to traverse a large and seemingly abandoned castle, stalked by otherworldly presences, set out on a mission dictated by a mysterious letter — from themselves.

With their previous release, the Penumbra duology, Frictional Games had succeeded in crafting a creepy and unique adventure which struggled at times to cultivate much mechanical engagement or depth, outside of the impressive and immersive physics simulation and interactivity. Using the same general template of these previous titles, especially Black Plague, here Frictional has streamlined and developed the format to create something more fully formed and independent. In terms of horror, The Dark Descent is a significant success as well. There's a number of notable chapters and set-pieces which succeed at unsettling the player, and the integration of chase sequences, similar to Penumbra’s, excel in contrast, due to strong and clear conveyance.

The puzzles benefit from this improved clarity as well. Given the stress the player will often be under, the presentation weaves a delicate balance between being impenetrably complex and being so straightforward as to patronize its audience. In its execution, the player often feels as though they’re barely scraping by, using their wits and observation, even as the path forward is never very out of the way, in reality. The combat and monster encounters are the same, generously providing the player with ample time to hide or escape, while impressing upon them the sensation of near-death experiences.

The writing and voice acting are excellent, as is Frictional’s developing standard, although the resolution of the story proves lackluster, diminishing in impact as it plays out. For their journey, the player is rewarded with a narratively satisfying, although underwhelmingly presented, climactic chapter. This feels like a step down from Black Plague, whose resolution was convoluted, sure, but ultimately satisfying in terms of pacing and presentation. On paper, Amnesia’s ending comes at the point in the story where it should, but with the trivial final encounter and unspectacular final reveals and story beats, the resolution feels limp and ordinary, as if the story simply arbitrarily ends. This issue permeates the entire game; while the visual design and ambience is immaculate —  as is the delicately woven backstory — the events you experience first-hand often feel unextraordinary. A lot of intrigue is built up as to what actions the player had taken part in before the events of the game proper… but as for those very in-game events, it’s often nothing to write home about, even as conceptually a great deal does happen. The result of this is a thematically rich story which struggles to compel the player to ask very many questions regarding those themes. In other words, a significant missed opportunity.

For most players, they’re looking into purchasing Amnesia: The Dark Descent for its horror elements, and those players will not be disappointed. There are portions of this game, such as the prison chapter, which, personally, were more frightening and paralyzing than any game I’d previously ever played. The story will impress, too, for those willing to put in the effort to understand it. Ultimately, The Dark Descent is an iteration on Penumbra which looks to refine and progress past the wrinkles of those releases’ ambitions. It has a few wrinkles of its own, but in terms of those desires, it’s an unqualified success, and the legacy and impact of its release can’t be understated.

I feel like more people should play/replay this today. I always hear people using TDD as a staple to compare other horror games to; as if it's a flawless masterpiece and the quality standard by which we should judge all other games in the genre. I wish they would take the time to remind themselves how the game actually feels to play now that it's over a decade old.

A:TDD is good. It's got tight controls, well put together ambience and atmosphere, stunning audio design, interesting and well delivered story, and a memorably identity of it's own in a genre quite over-saturated with low quality indie titles. The only real problem with it is, well, it's not particularly scary anymore. To the game's credit, this is almost entirely due to the gradual desensitisation of audiences to it's design elements, rather than any problems in the design itself.

Basically TDD was the game that created a lot of the moulds horror games have been using for the past decade, and as a result, what was once a fresh and unique experience has retroactively become just another by-the-numbers chasey hidey puzzle solving horror game. You have to give Frictional credit for creating, or at the very least popularising this style of horror game, but that credit won't help the game be scary again. It's a bittersweet irony that the game's immense success as a fresh new bone-chilling horror experience destined to revitalise it's genre is the very thing that's led to it being so predictable and sort of silly for modern horror audiences.

I still think it's great, of course. If you're not someone who plays horror games regularly and therefore aren't so versed in the usual genre clichés, maybe it'll still hold up for you in the spook department. For me though, I play horror games semi-regularly, and the only real sustainable factor in TDD nowadays is the story, which is worth it on it's own for sure, but the horror elements are too formulaic by 2023+ standards for it to fray any nerves.

As with any genre-defining game, you have to try to look at it from the perspective of it's time. Over the past 12+ years there have been thousands of games taking direct inspiration from it's influence. Impressive as it's legacy is, it has the inevitable consequence of wearing the unique elements of the original down as time goes on, and the end result is that TDD sadly feels quite generic when looked at from a modern perspective. I do wish more people made a habit of regularly replaying games like this, because it's hard to move in the horror sphere without seeing comparisons to older titles that, while effective horror experiences at the time, have since lost most, if not all of their edge with the eventual maturation of audiences.

It's a good game, marred by it's own influenced successors and their wider effects on the genre and it's audiences. Still worth playing because it's a piece of horror history, just don't be surprised if you end up having spontaneous shovel duels with the monsters for fun when you're meant to be running away.

[h1]”Don't forget, some things mustn't be forgotten. The shadow hunting me... I must hurry. My name is Daniel, I live in London at... at... Mayfair. What have I done? This is crazy. Don't forget, don't forget! I must stop him! Focus! My name is... is... I am Daniel.”[/h1]

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Amnesia: The Dark Descent is an atmospheric survival horror experience where Daniel, the character you play, is defenceless against the horrors he will face as he descends into the darkness of the castle.
But did Amnesia have enough oil in the lantern to stave off insanity, or was it lost to the abyss?

[tr]
    [td]🟩 An excellent horror atmosphere combined with how defenceless you are against enemies will keep you on the edge of your seat from start to finish.

🟩 Interesting world design coaxes you to explore resources and items and forces you to react quickly to some stressful situations that arise.

🟩 The physics allows for some fascinating puzzle mechanics.

🟩 Amnesia won't win any beauty awards as the dated graphics offer very little visually astounding, but this assists the atmosphere significantly. The grim castle architecture and blood-smeared walls definitely help define the experience from a visual standpoint. The audio is much the same, outdated yet enjoyable.[/td]
    [td]🟥 The enemy AI is pretty foolish. The monsters hunting you rely on surprise appearances and their speed to catch you.[/td]
[/tr]

[h1]Story[/h1]
The game casts you into the role of Daniel, a Londoner who awakens in the dark halls of the Prussian Brennenburg Castle. With little to no memory of himself or his past, all that he remembers is his name and that something sinister is hunting him.

Daniel sets off on his journey, dazed and confused, lost in the maze-like hallways of Brennenburg, until he comes across a note that he had apparently left for himself. The message details that he had forced himself to forget his past to preserve his innocence by utilising an amnesia potion. The letter goes on to urge Daniel to descend the castle in search of his host, a man named Alexander and to murder him and with one final warning that a "living nightmare" is chasing him and that he must find a way to escape because there are no means of fighting it.

Armed with this knowledge and a trusty lantern he was able to scrounge for, he sets off towards the depths of the dark, neglected castle, with horrors and nightmares on his heels.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2999878783

Amnesia: The Dark Descent does an exceptional job of immersing you in this story of deception, betrayal and discovery as Daniel descends into his own living nightmare. The plot is heavily reliant on you searching for and reading the notes scattered across the world, there is limited narrative to the game, and if you don't seek these out, you will be left wondering what is actually happening.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
[h3]The darkness, closing in.[/h3]
🟩 As you will quickly begin to understand as you progress through the story, light is your closest ally and worst enemy. It will protect you from losing your sanity as you wander the castle and witness the supernatural horrors that lurk within it, but you will also need to embrace the darkness to stay out of their sight. Managing this balance is entirely up to you.

🟩 Sanity is a very tangible resource in this game. It will fall as you witness supernatural events or if you spend too long looking at the horrors that roam the halls. The best way to manage this state is by sticking to the light. You can light candles and torches by utilising tinderboxes you can find scattered across the world or your lantern that requires oil to activate. Losing too much sanity causes your vision to blur and your senses to lose focus, and if left to fall totally will cause Daniel to collapse.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2999878703

🟥 The enemies are few and far between and mostly avoidable. They aren't very clever and follow some semblance of a scripted path. The best solution quite often is sitting in a dark corner for a few moments out of sight, and they'll usually get bored and walk away.

[h3]A chance to redeem yourself.[/h3]
🟩 When you're not running, hiding and avoiding the nightmares, you will likely find yourself completing puzzles. There are dozens of puzzles to solve across the castle grounds, ranging in intricacy from simple to sophisticated.

🟩 Many of them are actually remarkably inventive and amusing, especially the deceptively simple ones.

[h1]Audio and Visual[/h1]
As up above, Amnesia isn't going to blow you away with flashy graphics or astounding visuals. It does provide a gritty, atmospheric world that does immerse you in this living nightmare. Despite its dated graphics and design choices, the game still managed to attain a stifled gasp at some of the more stressful panic moments.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2999878456

The audio is actually far more impressive though it's also dated. It provides a fantastic overall ambience to the world, where every footfall raises your tension, and the creak of every door you wish would be silent rings loudly through the halls.

[h1]PC Performance and Specifications[/h1]
Amnesia is an old game, and it's safe to assume most anyone can run it with a somewhat recent computer.

There were no graphical issues to report.

I picked this up a few weeks ago and I got it on sale at a reasonably low price (2 euro something I believe) And man, what good value for money. If you're a horror fan, you can't pass on this one. 

You are Daniel, a man who awakes in a mysterious, gloomy castle. You don't know who you are, why you're in a castle, or what has exactly happened for you to loose your memory. You almost immediatly find a note however, which your past self wrote for you, before you lost your memory. It states: Your name is Daniel, you must stop Alexander, beware the shadow and remember that you chose to forget. Basically, you drank something with the intention of loosing your memory. You don't exactly know what drove you to do that, all the note says is that you chose to do it and that's all that matters.

As you venture onwards, and deeper into the castle, you eventually begin to piece together what is going on. You begin to rediscover what Alexander did, and why you must stop him. And you soon encounter the 'Shadow'. A mysterious creature that is following you, and is out to kill you. This monster shows up at different points in the game and when it does, you must avoid it. It is faster than you, you can't out run it. You can block up doors behind you to slow it down, and looking at the monster for too long can drive you insane! 

Other things can also cause you to loose your mind too: Standing in the dark and viewing disturbing things slowly begins to decay your sanity. When you loose your sanity, you drop to the floor and everything around you beings to change visually a slight bit. You can only move very slowly and you become very easy for the Monster to find. Avoiding insanity can be accomplished by not viewing the monster for too long, make sure you have your lantern out in dark areas or light up nearby torches on the walls and do not view certain other disturbing things for long periods of time.

The game is very atmospheric and the immersion is done ever so well. The game is always unsettling and you can really never trust it. You never truly know what is beyond the next door or around the next corner and I love this game for that.

Also the physics are a joy to behold, trust me on that one.

This game is great. It's super spooky, and I hope that's all anyone needs to know to play this game. 

With that said, I am incredibly interested in this game. It breaks a lot of rules you would think it would follow. It isn't Alien: Isolation or Resident Evil 7. The monsters are not always chasing you. There are scripted encounters and after they occur, the monster despawns. Pretty much every game I can imagine that has monsters that appear at certain points and disappear are not good. Most of those games use their scripted encounters to drop the monster right next to the player and force them to jump in a conspicuously placed designated hiding spot. While Amnesia does have a few hiding spots, they are few and far between. Largely the monster is dropped somewhere out of sight and freaks you out. That is the difference in a nutshell with this game: it doesn't want to kill you. If there was actually a monster hunting you down, then it is expected that you would actually get killed by the monster. I haven't played that much of Alien: Isolation, but a somewhat common criticism I see is how sometimes the horror of getting hunted by the Xenomorph can turn to frustration if you get killed by it and loose a bunch of progress. This game does the fear of the unknown very well by making it so there is just enough a threat that you are always wondering if it will pop out, but not so much of a threat that you'll die a bunch. Frankly, you could probably just hold sprint through pretty much the whole game and be okay. If you were caught, then you'll just respawn and the monster will be gone. Don't play like that, because it would be super lame. This game also has some wildly contradictory game mechanics that work very well with this game, but would be terrible in others. Sanity and lighting is the biggest instance of this. You loose sanity in the darkness, and don't loose sanity in the light. The monster can't see you in the darkness and can see you in the light. You can't look at the monster and keep your sanity, but you need to see the monster to know if it is close. If the monsters persisted or if dying sent you back to an earlier save, then these things would be an issue. Neither of those things are the case, so they aren't an issue. They just serve as a tense catch 22 that makes the game more upsetting. Hard mode changes some of that up, but playing hard mode after playing the regular game means you already understand enough about the game mechanics so that you don't have as hard of a time. Allegedly, I technically have not beaten hard mode. I played the last section and got mad that I kept dying to low sanity. There is an odd way to avoid dying, which I think is weird and it feels unintentional. 

Overall, this is a great game. Some of the scariest moments were when no monsters could even spawn, because everytime I would think to myself "Wow, I am scared and there aren't any monsters" I would immediately become even more scared by the prospect of a monster spawning.

Amnesia is my favourite horror game of all time, and one of my favourite games of all time. You have probably heard of this masterpiece, especially if you used YouTube at the start of the 2010´s. Brilliant game. In fact it might be one of the scariest ever. Like in Penumbra, there are enemies here (and they are creepier and more gruesome than ever), but they are scarce, leaving the immersive visuals and unsettling sound design to unnerve the hell out of you. Suggestion and fear of the unknown are key here, with a couple of shocking jump scares too. The stealth in Amnesia works well, with the ability to lure enemies away from where you need to go by, say, throwing rocks and creating diversions. Definitely a game to play at night alone, with no other sounds or distractions around.

Playing Amnesia: The Dark Descent in 2025 was an eye-opening experience. Despite its age, it stands tall among modern horror games. The gameplay feels polished, with physics-based interactions that remain impressive. While I’m not the biggest fan of puzzles, the game strikes a great balance. They’re neither too easy nor too hard, and they’re tied to the narrative in ways that make solving them rewarding.

The story is the heart of the game, delivered in a way that’s mysterious and compelling. It kept me curious throughout, as every note and memory revealed critical details. Paying close attention to the story isn’t just enriching, it’s essential. The narrative is layered with meaning, and small decisions can impact the outcome significantly.

While the game isn’t overwhelmingly scary, perhaps due to my higher scare tolerance, the tension is palpable. The NPCs are faster than you, so running is often your only option. This mechanic, coupled with the eerie atmosphere, keeps you on edge. One standout feature is the immediate feedback when solving puzzles, which subtly confirms you’re on the right track without breaking immersion.

It’s funny to think I discovered this classic through PewDiePie years ago. The rich story, creative gameplay, and immersive design make it a must-play, even today. Modern horror games could learn a lot from Amnesia’s creativity and depth.

Rating: 9/10. Playing it in 2025 was absolutely worth the time.

[b][i] Amnesia: The Dark Descent [/i][/b] is a hardcore survival horror game from 2010 developed by Frictional Games,the same guys who did the Penumbra series,so they have a reputation among indie/horror developers,along with years of experience on how to create seriously depressing and horrifying worlds. This review will be on the short side,because just about 15 thousand other people have said everything about this game,I am just here to put my two cents in,in fact,I feel obligated to write at least a few paragraphs,since this game deserves attention and respect,it is a staple and a benchmark by which all other horror games are judged. Basically it reformed and created a new sub-genre among horror games (and also because it took me 4 years to play it through,you can laugh now,yeah).

Now,I'm not gonna spoil the story for you,but rest assured,it is engaging,mysterious,and interesting enough to keep you on the edge of your seat throughout your descend into darkness. The Lovecraftian elements are obvious here, mixed with some heavy influence from Poe (namely the setting itself,among others). 
You are Daniel,an archeologist hailing from Britain,London. You wake up in the middle of the night in the castle of Brennenburg,located in East-Prussia. Hindered by amnesia (and probably some anxiety/paranoia),chased by an obscure shadow,your quest is to uncover a big mystery, what the hell happened to you,why are you in that old,decrepit place,and ultimately,to survive this living nightmare.

In the following section,we are going to take a look at the gameplay, the quality of the visuals/audio design,and the atmosphere.

The gameplay itself is simplistic yet your heart will probably skip a few beats. Seriously,this game is not for the faint of heart: you do not have means to defend yourself in any way,your only options are to either run,hide,or die. Your only friends are your trusty lantern and tinderboxes. You can utilize these in a way so that you won't go insane from total darkness surrounding the halls and passageways (at one point,torture chambers:p) of the castle. But beware,because if you stand in light,the monstrous creatures roaming the château will spot you with ease. There are the occasional puzzle segments,which are not too shabby,it gives you a little pause between discovering the place and shitting your pants.

With that out of the way,let's talk about the technical side of things: usually,when it comes to the graphics,I can be a little nitpicky,I'm not the "anything goes" type of guy,the visuals of a game can either immerse or put me off. Sometimes graphics don't matter,but we are talking about Amnesia,a game,in which the story is partially told and progressed with the medium of visuals. The guys do not disappoint,they did a stellar job in this department. I am not saying that the textures are Crysis/Shadow of Mordor/xy quality,but the way the game handles the lighting is nothing short of amazing.The atmosphere is heavy,crushing,morbid,other-worldly. It is mandatory to play this piece of art with the lights off,headphones on. 

Yes,headphones. If you are playing any other way,you deserve to get dragged out to the street and beaten with a stupid stick. The sound,music and the ambience is amazing. Men,women,children screaming in agony,the growl of monsters,walls cracking,wood creaking,chains rattling,inexplicable noises coming from the end of the pitch black hallway. It is all here. Enough said.


Ultimately,Amnesia is not just a game. It is a dark,terrifying tale to be experienced. If you think,you have the guts,the perseverance,and the love for the genre itself,go right ahead,enter Brennenburg. Just do not forget your name and your lantern.

It is not about the jumpscares. It is the pure psychological horror that messes with your head and makes you so scared that you need to stop a little before going forward, just to recover some of the sanity you left behind while playing it.

Finally after 7 years I was able to play this game through from start to finish!! Yaaaaaay! I am proud to say that I can now stand shoulder to shoulder with the other brave souls who have completed this title. *curtsey*

It's already been 8 years since release. It's amazing how this much time has passed and Amnesia is still one of the (if not the) scariest games in the world. And shamelessly, i hadn't played this amazing game up until this fall. I don't know why, but for some reasons i was constantly pushing Amnesia away. Until at some moment when i was bored, I decided to play it.
Before Amnesia Frictional Games wasn't really famous company and Penumbra was good, but niche game. Horrors are generally niche type of games, but Amnesia (and in some extent Outlast) managed to blow entire world and make those infinite youtube reactions and letsplays that made those games even more popular.  With all that said, i can't really undertstang all those people who say that Outalst is really scary and is one of the scariest games ever made. I played it and only few moments made me flinch. Wherease Amnesia scared sh*it out of me to the point i quit playing it for week. What's so scary in the game where you can easily run away from almost any monster and where there are almost zero non physical treats (that's about Outlast)? I do consider Outlast a decent game, but definitely not even top 5 of the scariest games. 
So what made Amnesia so scary and unique for so many players? I think it wasn't just one element of the game, but rather a combination of the elements of the game that worked together with one and only intent - to scare the player. I'll try to explain it a little.
Story: The story of the Amnesia is one of the things that isn't considered as one of the main elements of the game, but in my opinion, it was fitted in game really well and was one of the features that distinguished Amnesia from many other horror games, because some people think that horrors are all about trying to scary the player and not about the story itself. Plot in Amnesia is really interesting and was inspired by Lovecraft himself in some moments. You feel yourself involved in story. 
Soundtrack: Or, more specifically, sound design itself. Amnesia ost is pretty good on its own, but the best thing is sounds in the game. All those howls of wind and monster growls. The sanity loosing sound combined with Grunt theme is one hell of experience.
Atmosphere: One of the most exciting elements of the game. THAT and gameplay made Amnesia so unique. You know, wneh i start to remember, big, majestic castles aren't commonly used as element of the game. It's usually used as background. But in Amnesia it's part of the gameplay. You are interested in exploring the castle and reading all its secrets, trying to remember what your protagonist forgot and trying to hide from monsters. Speaking of which
Gameplay: The best and most detailed element of the game. THIS is why this game had become so popular, Unlike many other horror games Amnesia scares you in unordinary way. It's not just dumb jumpscares and crappy animations, but rather really well made combination of all elements of the game. The story, sound design, atmosphere, graphics (which is pretty good for not AAA game) and gameplay are working together to scare the player. That one thing that distinguishes Amnesia from other horror games is the fact that devs are scaring the player in multiple ways: sound, surrounding area, sanity system (so genius idea honestly) and really scary and disturbing monsters). That moment when Grunt was walking towards me under flashing light was one of the scariest moments in the entire gaming industry. Comparable to first encounter with Pyramid Head (that says a lot).
With all that said i just have to admit that Amnesia was really extraordinary experience and if you're fan of horror games you must check it out (although i think most players had already done that). It's one of those gems of gaming industry that was first of all made out of passion and creativity and not for money.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is that game you saw grown men scream at on Youtube. 

You play as Daniel, a man that has Amnesia. All Daniel remembers is that he has to kill some mook called Alexander, and to do that he must descend into the darkness of Brandenburg castle, find this goon, and make him cold.
A Dark Descent, if you will.

Hmmmm. 

Amnesia: The Spooky Spot is a first person horror game developed by Frictional Games. Everyone has this game, not many people played it, too scary, they get scared and go “Oof, that’s too scary for me, Chief.” Not me, though, I’m a big boy, I go to the bathroom standing up. Both ways. 

Some people consider this game the scariest game ever made, or at least one of the scariest. It was the big thing back in 2013 when it came out, all over the internet with facecam footage of people yelling at it. I didn’t get around to playing it to completion until just this year. Not because I was scared because, as stated before, I am a big boy who likes coffee with only a little bit of sugar and I only cried during Titanic when those band dudes were playing the sad song near the end. 

So is it THE SCARIEST GAME EVER MADE? I mean, its kind of spooky, sure. 

You need to understand that I haven’t felt anything since the Kennedy Assassination, and even then all I felt was recoil. I play horror games more for the atmosphere than I do the scary bits. And Amnesia has atmosphere in spades. Brandenburg Castle is a neat, moody place that’s fun to explore. It doesn’t let up through the entire game, and it actually manages to stay in the castle rather than, like, lets say teleport you to some alien location. 

Amnesia can be considered a modern take on the adventure game genre, in a way. You spend 100% of the time just exploring new places and solving puzzles. Well, thats not true, sometimes you have to hide from monsters as well. 

The monsters in Amnesia: Scary Decline are notorious at this point, but have you actually looked at one of these goofy fucks? The more common one looks like he had a handful of old school warheads and I feel like I can take the second one in a fight if I also get a sword arm and also maybe a gun. 

You have to manage both Danny’s physical health and mental health, but Daniel is kind of a paper puppet in human form. One time I cut his hand in a game event and it almost killed him. He’s also afraid of the dark, because he’s a sissy, which sucks because the darkness is super useful when enemies are looking for you, but that’s kind of the trade off, where you manage Daniel getting scared and taking damage to his mental health in return of being the sneakiest man to ever live. 

You take mental health damage from a bunch of things. Staying the dark for too long, looking directly at an abomination, seeing something upsetting like a pile of dead bodies or other spooky events. All of these take a tole on your brain until Daniel has a sort of melt down, falls over, and just kind of crawls around for a few seconds before brushing himself off and going on with his day.
Hey man, we’ve all been there. 

Oh, and you take physical damage by getting hurt. When you take too much damage you die. There you go, got that covered. 

I’ve only ever played two Frictional Games in my life, this and SOMA. And if I had to pick between them I’d probably go with this one. SOMA has a more interesting setting and themes, but Amnesia is kind of a more concise package. It doesn’t overstay its welcome and while it does screw around with cosmic horror and fun stuff like that, it never gets too psycho like other horror games tend to do. 

Remember the Second Suffering game? Remember the last quarter of the Second Suffering game? 

You do now. 

I liked Amnesia: The Gloomy Down-Escalator, though I doubt I’ll ever go back to it unless I’m streaming it or something like that. If you’re looking for a challenge then you might want to amp up the difficulty, because on normal its sort of a cake walk. I would recommend it for a single playthrough. You can usually get it on sale for pennies nowadays, but you most likely already have it.

You just haven’t played it.

Because you’re soft.
